name: Novatian
otherNames: Novatus, in Eusebius of Caesarea and Socrates of Constantinople
knownFor: A presbyter of Rome who refused to take back those who had sacrificed in the persecution under Decius, was made bishop against Cornelius in 251, and gave his name to strict churches that still kept his rule two centuries later; he also wrote On the Trinity.
dates: Made a rival bishop at Rome in 251
role: Presbyter of Rome, writer and rival bishop

keyWorks.title: On the Trinity
keyWorks.about: answers those who called Christ the Father himself and those who called him only a man. Jerome calls it a great volume, a sort of epitome of Tertullian's work, which many mistakenly ascribed to Cyprian of Carthage

keyWorks.title: On the Jewish Meats
keyWorks.about: a letter on the food laws, which Cleveland Coxe, the American editor, thinks was written during the persecution of Decius

traces: Made bishop by bishops who shared his view, he wrote to all the churches that those who had sacrificed should be urged to repent but kept from communion. Socrates of Constantinople says the provinces took sides: some thought the rule cruel, and others received it as just.

In 325 the Council of Nicaea, in its eighth canon, let the clergy of the Cathari, as his followers called themselves, keep their rank if they promised in writing to share communion with the twice married and with those who had lapsed in persecution and done penance.
Socrates says the Novatians of Phrygia and Paphlagonia kept their strict rule to his own day, and that at Rome they held many churches until Bishop Celestinus took them away.
remembered: Cornelius, bishop of Rome, wrote that the brethren were leaving Novatian every day and returning to the church.
Dionysius of Alexandria wrote to him that he ought to have suffered anything at all rather than split the church of God.
Cyprian of Carthage, who sided with Cornelius, wrote of him that whoever is not in the Church of Christ is not a Christian.
Socrates tells of the Novatian bishop Acesius at the Council of Nicaea, and of Constantine's answer to him, to set up a ladder and climb alone into heaven.
In Jerome's day many still read On the Trinity, though under the name of Cyprian.

uncertain: For the split, most of the account comes from his enemies: Cornelius, bishop of Rome, whose letter Eusebius of Caesarea keeps, and Cyprian of Carthage. Socrates of Constantinople, who gives Novatian's side, had a friend among the Novatians, Auxanon, an aged presbyter of their church. No letter of Novatian's own on the split survives; his case is known from Socrates's summary of his letter to the churches. Robert Wallis, who translated his works, says much of what is known of him comes only from his enemies, and Cleveland Coxe quotes Lardner that not one line of his own defense remains.

That three country bishops from a small corner of Italy were deceived, made drunk and forced to lay hands on him is Cornelius's charge, an enemy's. Socrates says only that bishops who shared his views made him bishop.

His rule against taking back those who had sacrificed is described by hostile witnesses as well as by Socrates. Cyprian mocks a rule that bids the fallen mourn and do penance and then die outside the church. Jerome says he refused to receive penitent apostates, and Eusebius that he held there was no hope of salvation for them.
Cornelius says he wanted the bishopric all along, though he swore he did not. Arthur McGiffert sees no reason to doubt Novatian's word, and thinks he may well have been urged against his will.

Cornelius says Novatian refused to come out of his room to help in the persecution, saying he admired another philosophy. McGiffert calls this a calumny. Neander suggested, McGiffert reports, that he had withdrawn to live as an ascetic.
Cornelius says he was baptized on his sickbed and made his followers swear at the Lord's Supper never to return to Cornelius. McGiffert accepts the sickbed baptism. The oath rests on Cornelius alone.
Socrates says he died a martyr under Valerian. Valesius, in a note to Socrates, disputed this: the Novatians' own book on his martyrdom was full of fables, he held, and made him only a confessor.

Socrates had the Acesius story from Auxanon, who went to Nicaea with Acesius, and says no other writer records it. Sozomen tells it after him. Some, among them Baronius, took Socrates for a Novatian. Valesius, followed by most later writers, held him only impartial.
The Greek writers call him Novatus. The book of 354 says that Novatus, coming from Africa, ordained Novatian outside the church at Rome; that Novatus, of Carthage, is another man.
The eighth canon of Nicaea does not name him. That the Cathari are his party rests on Eusebius and Jerome.
Nearly two centuries is reckoned from Socrates's own time, after the year 439, not stated by him.
That the Novatian churches spread east and west and lasted into the sixth century rests on Arthur McGiffert, in his notes to Eusebius.
McGiffert calls On the Trinity both able and orthodox. Cleveland Coxe reports that Cave dated it to about 257.
